h1: The 6 Best Printers for Remote Workers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Remote Workers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six home-office printers for remote workers compared on laser vs ink, scan and fax, running cost and footprint.
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer for remote workers, a compact monochrome laser with duplex, copy and scan. The HP OfficeJet Pro 8139 is the all-in-one with feeder and fax, the Epson EcoTank ET-2800 handles occasional color, and the Brother HL-L2405W prints text only. The Epson WF-2930 is the budget office, and the HP Smart Tank 5101 bundles two years of ink.
intro: Home printing habits are lumpy: nothing for two weeks, then a stack of forms in one afternoon. That pattern punishes the wrong printer type. An inkjet that rests for weeks can clog its nozzles and burn ink on cleaning cycles, whereas a laser's dry toner sits unchanged until you need it. Before comparing feeders, fax and apps, match the technology to how irregularly you print.

Eight wireless printers were considered and six ranked on print type, office functions, ink or toner cost and desk footprint. The order comes from spec sheets, not print tests. Remote workers also care about the unglamorous parts: whether a contract scans through a feeder, whether the printer joins a modern router, and how much shelf it demands when the desk doubles as a dining table.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: The lowest running cost for daily work, with copy and scan.
products.description:
The Brother DCP-L2640DW fits the way most remote workers print: invoices, contracts, the odd form, often unannounced. It is a wireless compact monochrome laser with duplex printing, copy and scan, mobile printing, Alexa support and a Refresh subscription trial, in the $200 to $500 band. Dry toner lasts through long idle spells, so the first page after a quiet month prints cleanly.

It ranks first because toner holds up far better than ink for steady daily printing. It also sits above the HL-L2405W by adding a scanner and copier, for a higher cost.

Buy it for a desk where documents are the daily load. The caveat is color: it prints black and white only, so presentations and marketing pages need another printer, and the price band is the highest in this ranking.

products.name: HP OfficeJet Pro 8139 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: Print, scan, copy and fax with a document feeder.
products.description:
HP's OfficeJet Pro 8139 is the all-in-one for people who handle paper. It is a wireless color inkjet with print, scan, copy and fax, an automatic document feeder, duplex printing and a 1-year Instant Ink trial, in the $100 to $200 range. The feeder is the practical gain: a ten-page contract scans in one go, without lifting the lid ten times.

It ranks second because it is the only pick with both a feeder and fax, and it gives color that the lasers cannot. Against the DCP-L2640DW, ink costs more over time than toner.

Buy it if you scan multipage documents regularly or still need fax for a client. The caveat is idle behavior: if you print only a few pages a month, ink may dry out, and the cleaning cycles waste ink. Heavy, steady printing suits the laser better.
products.skipIf: You print only a few pages a month.

products.name: Epson EcoTank ET-2800 Wireless Color All-in-One Supertank Printer
products.verdict: Color printing from refillable ink tanks, with no cartridges.
products.description:
The Epson EcoTank ET-2800 is the color choice for occasional jobs. It is a wireless color all-in-one with cartridge-free refillable ink tanks, and it prints, scans and copies, in the $100 to $200 range. Bottled ink costs far less per page than cartridges, which matters when a color presentation is a rare but large print job.

It ranks third because tanks lower ink cost for occasional color, while the body is larger than a compact laser.

Buy it for workers who print color slides and reports now and then. The caveat is space: leave desk room for the tanks, and note there is no document feeder, so multipage scanning means the glass.

products.name: Brother HL-L2405W Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: A simple laser for printing text and nothing else.
products.description:
Brother's HL-L2405W is the printer for people who only need text. It is a wireless compact monochrome laser with mobile printing, Alexa support and a Refresh subscription trial, in the $100 to $200 range. It prints, and that is it, which keeps the machine small and the setup simple.

It ranks fourth because it lacks the scanner and copier of the DCP-L2640DW, though it costs a band less. Single-function printers also have fewer parts to fail.

Buy it if you print only: reports, labels, shipping forms. The caveat is a hard limit: if you ever scan a receipt or copy an ID, you will need another device or a phone app, so pick the DCP-L2640DW or an all-in-one if that matters to you.

products.name: Epson Workforce WF-2930 Wireless All-in-One Printer
products.verdict: Scan, copy and fax with a feeder at a low price.
products.description:
The Epson Workforce WF-2930 is the budget office. It is a wireless all-in-one inkjet with print, scan, copy and fax, an automatic document feeder, duplex printing and a 1.4 inch color display, in the $50 to $100 range. A feeder and fax at this price are unusual, and the compact design suits a crowded desk.

It ranks fifth because cartridge ink costs more over time than the EcoTank models, though the low entry price is attractive. The small display shows menus but little guidance.

Buy it for a budget home office that needs office functions without the investment. The caveat is running cost: heavy printers will spend more on cartridges than the savings, so consider a tank model such as the ET-2800 if volume is high. Light users get the best value.

products.name: HP Smart Tank 5101 Wireless All-in-One Refillable Printer
products.verdict: Two years of ink included, but 2.4GHz Wi-Fi only.
products.description:
HP's Smart Tank 5101 attacks the ink problem. It is a wireless refillable all-in-one with print, scan and copy, two years of ink included and a cartridge-free tank design, in the $100 to $200 range. For a worker who prints weekly, two years of ink means the running cost is effectively prepaid.

It ranks last for one reason: it supports 2.4GHz wireless only, which can be a problem on modern routers or networks set to 5GHz only. It also lacks a document feeder.

Buy it if you want to forget about ink for two years. The caveat is the router: check your network band first, and confirm a dual-band setup exists. If your home network is 5GHz only, the printer will not connect.

whatMatters.detail: Lasers use dry toner that never clogs and suit steady document printing. Inkjets print color but can dry out if unused. Match the type to how often you print, not what you hope to print. Look for monochrome laser in the title if documents are the job, and for supertank if color matters, and ignore vague high-yield claims.

The cheap printer is not the cheap printing. Tank printers carry large ink reservoirs that lower per-page cost, and toner lasts for many pages. Check what is included in the box, such as the two years of ink with the HP Smart Tank 5101, and compare consumable prices before choosing a model, because refills are the long-term cost.

A flatbed scanner handles single pages, while an automatic feeder handles multipage contracts. Remote workers who sign and return documents benefit from a feeder. Look for ADF or auto document feeder in the specs, and note that the OfficeJet 8139 and WF-2930 list one while the Brother DCP-L2640DW does not, so paper-heavy desks should weigh that.

Some printers only join 2.4GHz networks, and routers set to 5GHz only will not see them. The Smart Tank 5101 is one. Confirm the band before buying, and check whether your router has a separate 2.4GHz network that you can enable for printer setup, then switch back afterward.

Tank printers are larger because of the ink tanks, while a compact laser fits a shelf. Measure the space first, including room to open the scanner lid and refill tanks. If your desk doubles as a table, a small footprint matters more than a bigger paper tray, and a shelf unit can free the surface.

faq.q: Can these print from my phone?
faq.a: The Brother models list mobile printing support. Most wireless printers here also work with phone apps, so check the maker's app list for your phone before buying and confirm the app supports your phone's version.

Cartridges are costly per page, and the price of a full set can rival the printer. The WF-2930 is a budget exception for light users, while a tank model like the ET-2800 or a toner laser gives lower running cost for steady printing, while a cartridge machine suits only occasional pages.

faq.q: Is the HP Smart Tank 5101 compatible with my router?
faq.a: It supports 2.4GHz wireless only, so a 5GHz-only router will not work. Many routers offer both bands, and you can enable 2.4GHz for printer setup. Check your router app for a split network option.

faq.q: How do I set up wirelessly?
faq.a: Use the maker's app, join your Wi-Fi network and install the driver on your computer. Follow the app prompts, then print a test page and send one scan to check the connection works.

faq.q: How do I prevent clogged ink?
faq.a: Print a page weekly. Lasers like the Brother DCP-L2640DW do not clog, so they suit irregular use better than inkjets, which can dry out in the nozzles and waste ink on cleaning cycles.
Few remote workers do. The HP OfficeJet Pro 8139 and Epson WF-2930 are the picks that include it. If you only e-sign documents, skip fax and save money, since a phone scan app covers the rest.

finalTake: Buy the Brother DCP-L2640DW if you print documents most days, or the HP OfficeJet Pro 8139 if multipage scanning and fax matter more than running cost. The ET-2800 suits occasional color, the HL-L2405W a text-only desk, and the WF-2930 a tight budget. Check your router band before choosing the Smart Tank 5101.
